The transcript belongs under the voice

It is the output of the thing directly above it. Beside the ring it read as a second panel competing for the same attention; under it, the screen has one axis and one order — question, mouth, words.

Why this question

D4's table is the design: studies have deadlines, work has clients, DSEC has other humans. Health, the job hunt and relationships have nobody. Asking what nobody chases you for gets the same answer without making you read a table.

Verbatim, including the mess

Lowercase, unpunctuated, false starts left in. A cleaned-up quote is not a quote, and the next screen has to be able to point at these exact words.

The clock counts up

Never down. D23: what the user says has no limit, ever — truncating it is the app grading your effort, which it does not do.

Night one

Three sentences out of what you said.

The interaction is the argument

Three rules drawn at once would be three pointers pointing at nothing. Watching the single rule move from one sentence to another is the scarcity rule demonstrated rather than asserted — and it costs one line of state.

The attribution is the mechanic

Every candidate carries the quote it came from, reproduced verbatim. It is the proof the sentence came out of your mouth rather than the model's. If the AI can't cite you, it doesn't get to propose it.

The rule is not explained anywhere

An earlier version of this screen carried a line about the underlined half being the part that can be false. It read as an instruction about how to think, on the screen where you are supposed to be choosing. The mark does the teaching on its own: by the third night you have noticed it only ever sits under the half that today can break.

The third one is the good one

doesn't renegotiate at half seven has a time and a place in it. You can see the kitchen. That is what D23 means by picturable, and it is why the messy transcript had to be kept intact.

A3

Make it yours, and commit

D9 ceremonyD4 28 days D20 ink bloom the flood amends D19 — not decided

The sentence is the screen. Edit it — the text is live — then hold the ring and don't let go. Three things on the whole surface: your claim, what committing costs you, and the hold.

Read this before you like the flood

D19 gives accent one use only, and DESIGN.md closes the list in as many words: the emphasis mark, plus the ring contour while your thumb is down — “That is the complete list.” A full-window accent field is a third use and by far the largest. It is not an application of D19; it is a proposed amendment to it, and this page has no authority to make that call.

DESIGN.md already refused a smaller version of this move. A full-bleed illustration in accent is listed as not decided, on the grounds that it “would put more of that colour on one screen than the rest of the app uses in a month.” A whole window is more than that again.

The case for it is D16's generating principle — what repeats must be abstract or absent; what is rare can be vivid — and this fires about thirteen times a year. The case against is that D19's whole discipline is that the colour points at one thing. If you want it, it goes into FORCE-V2 as a numbered change to D19 with its reasoning. If you don't, the same ceremony runs in ink and it costs nothing.

Committing

Committed.

Day 1 of 28. Tomorrow morning it's waiting for you.

The flood is the ceremony

Accent grows out from under your thumb until it has taken the whole window, then drops to the ground colour as the word arrives. It is the only time in the product that colour fills a screen — which is exactly why it can only happen once per pursuit.

The sentence inverts under the colour

Two copies of the screen, pixel-aligned: the normal one, and the same words in bg clipped to exactly the circle the flood has reached. So the sentence doesn't get covered — it turns over as the colour arrives, and the boundary is the edge of the circle.

knowingly breaks D17 bg on accent measures 3.87:1, and ink on it is 4.07:1. Nothing passes 4.5:1 on that orange — not white, not black, not pure #000, which only reaches 4.30:1. So this is the one place in Force where the legibility floor is broken on purpose, for about four seconds, on a sentence you wrote and were reading a moment earlier.

If that is not acceptable, the arithmetic says what to do: lighten the flood past a relative luminance of 0.20 and dark text clears 4.5:1, or darken it below 0.144 and ink clears it. Either is a change to D19, which is the same call the flood itself needs.

Five and a half seconds, and it remembers

Long enough that you cannot do it while thinking about something else. Release and it falls back over ~2.4 s — slower than it filled, because backing out should not feel like a slap — and it never resets, so two short holds add up to one long one.

The rule gets out of the way first

The emphasis rule retracts the moment the hold starts, so the accent field and the accent mark are never on screen together. Otherwise the first half-second of every commit would be two accents at once, which is the thing D19 exists to prevent.

The numeral had to go

A 46 px 28 under the claim made the length of the pursuit the loudest thing on the screen. The commitment is the sentence; 28 is a condition attached to it, so it is one line of body text directly beneath.

Why a hold and not a button

A click is indistinguishable from dismissing a dialog. ~1.2 seconds is the smallest act that cannot be done by accident — and letting go early shrinks the circle back, so backing out is as visible as going through.

raised, not resolved The strict-mode line came off this screen at your request. D12 requires it be mentioned once at onboarding, so it has to land somewhere — it is now the quiet footer on A4. If you want it gone entirely, that is a change to D12 and goes in the record.

The other two — and no, it doesn't repeat

D4 one + two not in the recordD12 the one mention

You asked whether A2 loops until there are three. It doesn't, and it shouldn't — three holds on night one is three ceremonies, and a ceremony you perform three times in five minutes is a form. One claim is committed. The other two are named and then left alone. They came out of the same yap, they carry the same attribution, and they never get a gate.

Why one hold and not three

D4 says the primary is chosen by what your mind is most willing to quietly drop — which means exactly one of the three is the one you'd lose. Committing all three with the same weight is a way of admitting you haven't picked.

A background claim that could be settled is a second gate wearing a smaller hat. These are read, not answered. They surface again with their own evidence, and at day 7 and day 28.

“just the one for now” is a real exit

Someone whose yap produced only one honest answer should not be handed two more to carry. The screen offers, it does not fill quotas.

this is a proposal FORCE-V2 does not say how the two background claims get created. D4 fixes that there are up to two; D9 describes night one as picking one and stops there. Everything on this screen is my reading, not a decision — and it needs to become one, because B1's morning beat already shows two of them standing.

Section B

The loop — two beats, one gate

A ~10-second morning briefing with no lock, and a 60–90 second evening beat that is the wall (D5). v1 ran 6–9 gates a day in week one and that is the direct cause of I scrolled through without reading. Scarcity is the entire mechanism: one gate a day, exactly one, and it fires when you close the day rather than when a clock says so.

Speaking — the moving line

replaces D20's layered ring — amends D20 D19 accent, transientD3 spoken floor

One line, pinned at both ends. A carrier oscillation gives it the shape of a wave; your voice is its amplitude, read out of a rolling ~2.3 s history — so what you said half a second ago is still travelling along it. It is the accent rule from under your claim, doing a second job: while you speak, the rule stands down and the line takes its colour, so there is still exactly one accent thing on the screen.

D20 locks the layered ring, and this is not it. Swapping the ring for the line is an amendment that goes into FORCE-V2 with its reasoning. The ring is still built and still correct — it is the first panel in B3b, so you can put them side by side before deciding.

Amplitude, not decoration

Driven by RMS per buffer converted to dBFS, floored at −58 dB, gamma-shaped, then smoothed with an asymmetric attack and release — 26/s up, 8.5/s down. That asymmetry is most of why a meter reads as voice rather than as noise.

Your syllables travel along it

The line samples a rolling ~2.3 s of history across its width, so the left end is what you are saying now and the right end is where it has got to. A pause shows up as a flat stretch moving across, which is the one thing a level meter cannot show you.

Pinned at both ends

The envelope goes to zero at both edges. A line that runs off the frame is a waveform in a media player; a line that starts and ends inside the panel is a mark someone made.

The rule stands down

The accent under the falsifiable clause retracts the moment the line comes alive, and returns when you stop. One accent on the screen at a time, which is the whole of D19's discipline and the reason this swap does not cost anything chromatically.

This page has no microphone, so the envelope is synthesised with speech-like bursts. The smoothing is the real thing: RMS per buffer to dBFS, floored at −58 dB, gamma-shaped, asymmetric attack and release at 26/s up and 8.5/s down. That asymmetry is most of why a meter reads as voice rather than as noise.

B3b

Hold to speak — four other ways

D20 locks the ring — these would amend it new

All five run off the same amplitude engine — the real one, RMS to dBFS, floored at −58 dB, asymmetric attack and release at 26/s up and 8.5/s down. Only the instrument changes. Hover any panel to make it speak. The question to hold each one against: on night twenty, is this something you look at, or something you have stopped seeing?

1 · The layered ring D20

Three solid bodies, back to front. The one that exists.

2 · The rule typographic

…went anyway, didn't want to

The emphasis mark, extended. Your voice draws the line under your own words as you say them.

3 · The breath no meter at all

I am someone who trains when I don't feel like it.

Nothing new on the screen. The sentence's own weight and optical size move with your voice — the variable font is the instrument.

4 · The column history, not level

Every second you have spoken, stacked and scrolling up. You can see the shape of the whole answer, including the pauses.

5 · The well duration

The ground itself rises while you keep going, and the surface moves with your voice. Stop, and it holds where it got to.

How to judge these

Not “which looks best.” Force runs this ~340 times a year, so the only question that matters is which one you would still be glad to see on night twenty.

Every one of them is quiet on purpose. This is the screen you face at 11pm on a bad day, and it has to be the sentence and your voice — nothing else asking to be looked at.

What each one is actually saying to you

The ring says you are being taken in. It is an object that exists while you speak and stops existing when you stop. Its weakness is that it is a circle, and every voice interface on earth is a circle.

The rule says this is being written down. It is the only one that reuses a mark Force already has — the accent rule under the falsifiable clause — so it costs no new visual vocabulary. It is also the quietest, which on night twenty may be the whole argument.

The breath says the sentence is listening. Nothing is added to the screen at all; the claim you are defending is the thing that moves. It is the most distinctive option and the most fragile: it needs the variable-font axes pinned per frame, it can read as a rendering fault if overdone, and there is no affordance telling a new user their microphone is live.

The column says look how much you said. It is the only one with memory — the pauses are visible, and a four-word night looks obviously different from a ninety-second one. That is either honest feedback or quiet grading, and D3 forbids the second.

The well says keep going. It rewards duration, which is the one thing this app must never ask for. Included because it is the most seductive of the five and I think it is wrong: a screen that fills up when you talk longer teaches you to talk longer, and D3's floor is one sentence in your own words, not a word count.

Where this stands against the record

D20 locks the layered ring. Nothing here overrides that, and the gate screens in B2, B3 and F3 all still use it. These four exist because you asked to see other directions, and swapping any of them in is an amendment to D20 that goes into FORCE-V2 with its reasoning.

If it were mine to call I would take the rule, and I would keep the ring for night one only — the yap is the one moment where a big obvious "you are recording" object earns its place, and by night twenty the rule is the one you would still be happy to see. But the test is the one at the top of this plate, and you are the one who has to face it at 11pm.

Settling — Fling

D20 flingD7 three states D12 silence

Pick the mark up and throw it. Real spring physics integrated per frame — no CSS curve, no Curve, nothing eased. The fling velocity goes straight into the spring, so a hard throw overshoots and a gentle one does not. There is a 620 ms window before it commits, and changing your mind inside it redirects rather than restarts.

Underdamped, once, then still

A few percent of overshoot, one time, and at rest fast enough that you are not waiting on it. Two overshoots or a visible wobble has left D20 regardless of what the numbers say. The constants are not written here on purpose — they live in settle_scene.dart and a number copied into prose is wrong the first afternoon someone tunes it.

Why it must be a throw

This is the piece that makes the settle an act rather than a confirmation. A broken day you threw into the strip lands differently from one you placed there — and you did that, not the app.

Then the app says nothing

The mark lands and the panel goes. No closing line, no summary, no "see you tomorrow". Under Principle 3 there is nothing in the record tonight that is worth a sentence, and silence is the default output, not the fallback.

Flutter's own spring can't do this — animateWith(SpringSimulation) cannot retarget mid-flight, which is the entire reason to use a spring. Force writes its own simulation clock seeded from current position and velocity.

The exit is a statement, not a dismissal

It says Not tonight. It does not say Skip, Close, Later, Maybe tomorrow or Remind me. Those are all ways of not answering; this is an answer.

unsettled is not broken

Broken means you showed up and lost. Unsettled means you didn't show up. Conflating them corrupts the record — and unsettled is the more diagnostic of the two, because a run of unsettled days is the app dying, and that is the one thing v1 could never see about itself.

The machine is never locked

macOS offers windowShouldClose → false and .terminateCancel; the strict-mode spike verified both work. Force does not take them. A gate blocking a machine you earn money on is a hostage situation with your income attached — and v1's // the "no escape" rule produced exactly one outcome: total escape.

Wednesday · day 20

Yesterday didn't settle. Bad day, or busy day?

two taps and it's closed

Why two buttons and not a microphone

This is a repair, not a beat. Re-showing last night's question builds a nag, and asking someone to speak about a day they already declined to speak about is the same question in a costume.

The two answers go different places

Bad day is a day that happened and hurt — the record keeps it and the app says nothing more. Busy day is the app's own early warning: two of those in a row and the gate is arriving at a time that doesn't fit your life, which is a problem with the schedule, not with you.

Nothing happens after one

D12: on a first miss, genuinely nothing. No colour change, no "streak broken", no gentle reminder. This screen is the entire response.

Section C

When it stops being a whisper

Nothing, then a question, then a trial (D12). Most nights the gate is one prompt and thirty seconds. It opens into a real conversation only on the five triggers in D6 — the day settled broken, the testimony was vague, Tempo contradicts you, it's a second consecutive miss, or the 28-day review is due. Every one of those is a moment where a human who cared about you would say something. On every other night it shuts up, and that is precisely what buys it the right not to.

D12 nothingD19 no reaction

Left: the night after a day you kept. Right: the night after a day you broke. They are pixel-identical apart from one 11 px mark in the strip, which is the record, not a reaction. If one bad day produces any visible response, you learn the app is watching for failure — and the cheapest way to avoid a reaction is to stop opening it. That is exactly how v1 ended. Both frames are cropped to the part that differs — the type, the marks and the spacing inside them are at 1:1 like everywhere else.

The claim is wrong

Both exits are real

Miscalibrated claim → rewrite the wording, always free (D4). Hostile week → name it, and the app genuinely backs off. If the week is wrong led to more pushing it would be a fake option, and one fake option poisons every other choice the app offers.

Still not a trial of you

Stopping early — the receipt

D4 receiptD23 D14 native only

This screen carries the exact sentence that produced D23. It is the only place in the product where the app argues for staying, and it does it without a single verb aimed at you.

Stopping

You started this 19 days ago. You've gone on 11 of them. There are 9 days left.

Stop now and you never find out if it would have stuck.

say what the evidence showed and why you're stopping

The rejected version, kept on purpose

Drop it now and you're not deprioritising a habit — you're retiring a claim four days early, without the receipt.

Three abstractions in twenty-three words. You cannot see a deprioritisation. There is a number in it — four days early — and it does no work, because it hangs off the end of a concept you have already stopped parsing. Concreteness is not "contains a digit".

Why the shipped one works

19, 11, 9 — front-loaded, in the order you would count them, each one a fact only your record contains. Then a stake you can picture: a future you can see yourself not having. And it never tells you to stay.

You cannot do this from a keyboard

D14 makes retiring native-only, and the receipt rule does half the work on its own — exiting requires a microphone, because it requires you to say it.

Section D

The reviews

The only two surfaces where the app is allowed to go long, because they are the only two you sat down for. D23's rule underneath the whole length table: the app's own prose is short on surfaces it forced you onto and long on surfaces you chose. The gate is forced. A review is chosen. That is the only variable — and it is why illustration is permitted here and banned on the gate.

Why the illustration is allowed here

What repeats must be abstract or absent; what is rare can be vivid. The per-claim engraving regenerates every 28 days — roughly thirteen images a year, each made from a sentence you wrote and something you said out loud.

It inherits the palette

The engraving is black line art on white, knocked out by using its own luminance as the alpha channel and then recoloured to ink3. Not a segmentation model: matting eats thin hatch lines, and cross-hatching is the entire style.

Counts, never a score

19 / 6 / 3 are three numbers side by side. There is no percentage, no grade, no comparison to last window. An AI that scores you becomes an opponent you game or resent — and you can lie to it for free.

The one line the record earns

You came back on the 4th without anyone asking you to is true because of D12: on a first and second miss the app said nothing. The silence earlier is what makes this sentence available now.

Stopping is still free of shame

It sits in the same list, in the same type, as keeping. D4 wants the receipt because a log of what you've abandoned and why is the most useful document about you that could exist — not as punishment.

Why the marks wrap at 14

28 marks at 29 px each is 812 px, and the day numbers are 14 px and do not shrink to fit — so the row has to break. It breaks at 14 rather than wherever the container runs out, which makes each row a fortnight and the two halves of the window directly comparable. D17 forced the break; putting it somewhere meaningful was free.

Section E

Reading the record

The same data on two machines with two different jobs. D14 draws the line in one place and it is structural rather than a policy: the web API has no endpoint that can write a day's verdict. There is nothing to disable, because there is nothing to call. If you could settle a day in a browser tab you would settle it half-watching something else — reflex-ticking with extra steps, which is v1's death reproduced faithfully in a new medium.

Section F

The rest of the product

The Counsel is in v1 scope (D22), late in the order for a product reason rather than a scope one — the Loop is what makes it unfakeable, so it cannot come first. Settings is where strict mode lives and where the app has to be honest about what an operating system will and will not let it do.

F1

The Counsel

D22 in v1 scopeD23 goes long register undecided

For when you're stuck. Any chatbot can debate two options; only Force can say you've claimed this for 19 days and defended it on 11. You opened this, so it is allowed to take its time.

Force — the Counsel
You said

i've got the gym thing and the job applications and i can only actually defend one this week.

You've claimed the gym for 19 days and defended it on 11. You have never made a claim about applications at all — so there is no record to argue from, only an intention.

That asymmetry is the whole answer, and it cuts the way you probably don't want. The gym claim has already survived a 4-day gap and come back. It is the only evidence you own that you can restart something after dropping it. Applications have never been tested, so you don't know whether you drop them on day 3 or day 12, and you won't find out by protecting the thing that already works.

If you defend applications this week, the gym drops to background and stays visible every morning without a gate. You find out in 7 days whether 11 out of 19 was the claim working or the novelty working. That is the more useful week and it is the more expensive one.

If you defend the gym, you keep a run that is already proven and you learn nothing new about yourself.

Both of those are real. You pick.

Nothing here changes a claim. Starting and stopping happen at the gate.

It argues, then stops

Both of those are real. You pick. The app states the position and stops — D23's rule, and the reason the last line has no verb aimed at you.

The acceptance test lives here

Your words: You should not be the one helping me organise my thoughts. Force should be. This is the surface where that either happens or doesn't, and it only works because the Loop fed it 19 days of evidence first.

What it refuses to say

No recommendation dressed as a fact, no confidence score, no "based on your patterns I'd suggest". Every sentence above is either a count from the record or a consequence you can check.

not in the record The Counsel's register — how blunt it is, and whether it differs from the gate's — is listed as undecided in COPY.md. This draft is deliberately blunter than the gate. Tell me if that is wrong before it becomes a decision.

F2

Settings — and being honest about strict mode

D18D12 never auto-offered D8 4am boundaryCOPY §10

Force may never claim you cannot get past it. That is sourced, not stylistic: on Android any foreground app calling setHideOverlayWindows(true) — Settings does, and so do system permission dialogs — makes the gate vanish. On macOS kill -TERM always wins, and Force Quit and Activity Monitor both go through that path. Copy promising an inescapable gate would be a lie about the exact property D7 spent its whole argument removing.

Force — settings
The day

The day turns over at 4am

an 11pm session and a 1:30am one belong to the same day

4:00
Voice

Play each one before you pick. One tap stops it mid-sentence, always.

Strict mode

A panel covers the screen from the time you set until the day settles.

What it can't do, on each machine:

macOS — the panel sits over a full-screen app without taking focus or switching Spaces. Force Quit still quits it. Nothing here locks the machine.

Android — opening Settings hides the panel. That's the operating system, not a bug, and there is no version of this app that gets around it.

iOS — there is no panel. The system draws its own shield over apps you choose, and Force never comes forward at all.

Turn this on because you want it. It won't be suggested to you after a bad night.

Your voice recordings

Transcribed on this machine, then the audio is deleted. The words are kept; the recording isn't.

The limits are the feature

Printing what strict mode cannot do is the only version of this screen that survives contact with a user who tries it. The first time someone escapes a gate that promised to be inescapable, every other sentence in the app loses credit.

4am, stated in lived terms

D8's boundary is explained as an 11pm session and a 1:30am one belong to the same day rather than as a configuration value. Shifts are chaos; the clock has to match the life.

Four voices, chosen for stance

Warm / flat / dry / hard. Gender and accent fall out of the stance rather than driving it, and you hear each one before choosing instead of reading an adjective.

default assumed Discarding audio after transcription is my assumed default, not a decision in the record. It has to be stated on this screen either way, because users have to be told.

Some claims can't be on a screen that appears over whatever you're doing. The gate is a panel that arrives at 11pm wherever you are — on a train, in a shared flat, with someone reading over your shoulder. What it has to be, for it to be worth anything

It never appears at the gate. The evening gate is a panel at screen-saver level that arrives over whatever is on your display — that is D18's whole design, and it is precisely why a private claim cannot be on it. Private claims settle inside private mode, when you go there. That is not a second gate; D5's one-gate rule is about the thing that interrupts you, and this never interrupts.

Nothing about it leaks into the surfaces that aren't private. Not the morning beat, not the record, not the web dashboard, not a notification, not the Counsel — unless you are inside private mode when you ask. The closed state above names no sentence and shows no count, because a count is information too.

The model context is separate. Whatever the AI knows about a private claim is not available to it when it is writing your ordinary evening line. Otherwise the app says something true and unexplainable on a shared screen, which is worse than saying nothing.

No illustration. D16 generates a per-claim engraving every 28 days and puts it on the record. A private claim gets none — or gets one that only exists inside private mode. Undecided, but it cannot be the current behaviour.

The one that is a real fork, and it is yours to call

FORCE-V2 §1b says state syncs to a server, and that was a deliberate choice — cloud sync and restore. Private claims put that under pressure: the reason to keep something private is usually not "hide it from my flatmate" alone.

Two honest options. Device-only — private claims never leave the machine, which means no sync, no restore, and if you lose the laptop you lose that record. Simple, and the promise is easy to keep. End-to-end encrypted — they sync, but the key is derived on-device and the server holds ciphertext it cannot read; restore works if you still have the key. More work, and the honest version of it means the web dashboard can never show them either, because the browser would need the key.

I would take device-only for v1 and say so plainly in the UI, because a privacy promise you can explain in one sentence is worth more than one you can only explain in a paragraph. But this is a decision with a real cost either way and it goes in the record with its reasoning.

Section G

Verification

v1 shipped colours nobody had measured and the failures surfaced seven months later, in a spike, by accident. So the checks below run in your browser against the screens you just scrolled past — they read the rendered pixels rather than quoting the design doc. If a plate above drifts, the numbers here go red on their own.

G1

Contrast, measured on this page

D17WCAG 2.1 sRGB

Every row samples a real element from the screens above — its computed colour against its computed background, walked up the tree until something opaque is found.

Two rows clear their floor and would fail a different one, which is the whole reason they are marks rather than type. broken #8A7566 at 4.34:1 and accent #B4553A at 3.87:1 both pass 3:1 and both miss 4.5:1 — so any text that names a broken day is written in ink2, and the emphasised words stay ink while the accent lives in the rule beneath them. That is arithmetic on a locked palette, not a taste call.

Watch ink3 on a raised surface: 4.62:1, with 0.12 of headroom. Do not stack it on bg2 and then also reduce its opacity or dim it on selection — there is nothing left to spend. The showcase hit this exact wall, and its answer is the right one: the strip does not dim on selection at all; selection is carried by a halo and by size, which cost no contrast.

One genuine miss, and it is the one on the list below: unsettled #5A6066 at 2.97:1, which is 0.03 under the 3:1 floor.

G2

Where accent appears — counted, not claimed

D19 one use

D19 gives accent #B4553A exactly one resting use in the entire product: the emphasis mark on the falsifiable half of the claim. The moment it appears twice on one screen it stops pointing at anything. This walks every element on the page and counts what actually resolved to that value.

The page chrome — headings, rails, chips, buttons, tables, this callout — uses no accent at all. The only two places it appears outside a screen are the swatch in the token grid and the swatch in G1's table, where the colour is the subject rather than the styling. That was a constraint on building the page, not a coincidence, and it is what makes the count mean something: if the surrounding document had spent the colour on a link or a highlight, the table above would be measuring nothing.

One appearance cannot be counted from the DOM and is declared here instead: the innermost contour of the hold-to-speak ring is drawn to a canvas and borrows accent for as long as the thumb is down. That is the transient exception DESIGN.md records, and with it DESIGN.md closes the enumeration in as many words — “That is the complete list.”

And one thing the table cannot see, which is not settled

The commit flood on A3 takes the whole window in accent. The table above does not count it because it sits at scale(0) until you hold the ring and zero painted area is zero ink — but that is a measurement convention, not permission. D19 says accent has one use. A full-window field is a third use and the largest by three orders of magnitude, so it is a proposed amendment to D19, not an application of it. It is drawn on A3 with the argument on both sides, and it is in H5 as open.

This is the failure mode this whole section exists to catch, and it caught me: I built the thing, wrote it up as though the record permitted it, and had to be told. A census that its author can quietly define his way out of is not a census.

G3

The variable-font trap

DESIGN.md · the sharpest edge in the port

Fraunces' fvar default instance is wght 900 / opsz 9 — Black, at caption optical size. Flutter instantiates that default. Ask for a 30 px claim without saying otherwise and you get this, with no error, no log line and no missing-glyph box:

Unpinned — the fvar default

I am someone who trains when I don't feel like it.

wght 900 · opsz 9 · 30px

Pinned, as every TextStyle must be

I am someone who trains when I don't feel like it.

wght 430 · opsz 30 · 30px

CoreText did optical-size mapping for free on the SwiftUI build. Flutter does not, and there is nothing to turn on. A style without fontVariations is a bug, not a default — pin wght and opsz on every single one, with opsz set to the pixel size.

Both panels above are the same font file at the same 30 px. The difference is two numbers. This page pins every style the same way the Dart will have to.

G5

The four motions, isolated

D20

House curve is cubic-bezier(.16, 1, .3, 1) — fast out of the gate, long tail. Nothing in Force overshoots except the settle, which earns it. A panel that bounces open teaches you that things in Force bounce, and then the one mark a night that is supposed to land with weight lands like everything else does.

1 · Ink Bloom — 1.15s

I am someone who trains when I don't feel like it.

Whole sentence out of blur at once. No stagger: the claim is one thought, and a reveal you have already seen nineteen times is a wait.

2 · Italic + rule — 0.72s

I am someone who trains when I don't feel like it.

Begins 0.9s after the bloom settles. The gap is the point — the sentence is read whole first, then the app puts its finger on the half that can break.

3 · The layered ring

Three solid bodies, back to front. Depth from overlap and occlusion, never a gradient.

4 · Fling
Kept
Broken

A spring, not a duration. It ends when it stops.

Measured, with the caveats stated

Over a 6.5-minute auto-drive of all six showcase scenes: 14,884 frames, zero exceptions, zero layout overflows. 22 frames (0.15%) over the 120 Hz budget, 3 frames (0.02%) over 60 Hz. Memory plateaued and then declined — 355.8 MB peak, 262.8 MB at the end, flat to within 0.3 MB over the final 90 s.

Both caveats from the spike's own notes: the iOS Simulator vsyncs at 60 Hz, so 120 Hz headroom is an inference rather than a measurement; and these are debug-mode numbers. Neither closes without a physical ProMotion device.

What is faithful here and what isn't

The bloom technique, the 0.9s gap, the ring's smoothing constants and the spring's shape are the real ones. The ring's amplitude is synthesised because a web page has no microphone, and the spring integrates in JavaScript rather than Dart.

Section H

Not decided

Everything below is open on purpose. None of it is drawn as though it were settled, and none of it should be resolved by someone quietly picking one and building it. Two of these block code: a verdict added after days exist is a migration and a palette change, and a stroke width chosen by accident is how v1 shipped a 1.72:1 mark.

H1

Is there a fourth verdict?

blocks the enumD5 vs D7

D5 says the day settles as kept / partial / broken. D7, the palette note in FORCE-V2 §4 and spikes/SPEC.md all say kept / broken / unsettled. Three places against one, and D7 is the later and more worked-out decision — but partial was never explicitly retracted. Every screen on this page is drawn with three states. A fourth mark needs an eleventh token or a split fill. At 11 px the split reads as a smudge, so the mark grows — and the mark size is what sets the strip's whole geometry.

What it needs from you

My read: partial is a leftover from before D7 existed, and D7's argument actively works against it — the value of the record is that unsettled is not broken, and a fourth state that means "sort of kept" gives every ambiguous night a place to hide. A day that closes as broken, spoken honestly, is worth more than a day that closes as kept; a day that closes as partial is worth almost nothing, because nobody ever has to say what actually happened.

But this is D5's word against D7's and it is your call, not mine. It has to be made before the enum exists: adding a state after days are on disk is a migration and a palette change at the same time.

Three ways out, and they are not equivalent

Carry it with stroke weight — the showcase's own fix, 1.4 px to 1.6 px. Cheapest, keeps D19 untouched, and the middle panel above is what every screen on this page already uses.

Fill it solid — passes comfortably, but then unsettled and broken are both filled discs and the open ring stops carrying "you didn't show up". The shape is doing real work; I would not spend it.

Whichever way it goes: measure it and write the number down. That is the whole difference between this and how v1 shipped.

H3

Fraunces Italic is not in the repo

found while building thisD20 italic + rule

D20 locks the emphasis as italic and a rule. Both font directories — force-old/…/Resources/Fonts/ and spikes/flutter-showcase/assets/fonts/ — contain exactly one Fraunces file, and its axes are opsz, wght, SOFT, WONK. There is no ital axis. Fraunces ships italic as a separate file and nobody has ever added it.

Real italic — the file I fetched

I am someone who trains when I don't feel like it.

Synthesised oblique — roman, skewed

I am someone who trains when I don't feel like it.

The left has true italic letterforms — a single-storey a, a different f, narrower fitting. The right is the roman leaning over, and on a serif that reads as a rendering fault rather than as emphasis. This is a five-minute fix, but it is only five minutes if someone notices before the Dart is written rather than after the first screenshot looks slightly wrong.

Fix: add Fraunces-Italic[SOFT,WONK,opsz,wght].ttf from google/fonts/ofl/fraunces to the app's font assets and declare it as the italic style of the same family. It is already downloaded into this session's scratchpad, and this page is rendering it.

Untested and load-bearing

Real NSWorkspace.didWakeNotification — the exact event that killed v1 — has never been triggered; the spike could not do it without sudo, and spikes/strict-mode/evidence/macos-events.log is wired to catch it. Also unverified: physical Android hardware, OEM battery-killer behaviour, Play policy on SYSTEM_ALERT_WINDOW, sustained animation on a real 120 Hz device, and the Windows build, which needs CI.

Not a design question, but it blocks D21

The repo is not a git repository. force-old/ carries its own .git; the root has none. D21 is GitHub + Developer ID, signed and notarised, so this has to happen before anything ships and it should happen before the first Dart file exists, not after.
